name: Phil Weiser

summary.text: Lesley Dahlkemper is a member of the Jefferson County Board of County Commissioners and formerly served as the board's chair; she was elected to her second four-year term in November 2022.
Phil Weiser is the Attorney General of Colorado, first elected in 2018 and now in his second term; he lives in Denver.
Before becoming attorney general, he was dean of the University of Colorado Law School and worked in the Clinton and Obama administrations, including as a deputy assistant U.S. attorney general.

experience.text: Dean, University of Colorado Law School, 2011-2016.

Deputy assistant U.S. attorney general, Justice Department Antitrust Division, and senior advisor for technology and innovation at the White House National Economic Council, during the Obama administration.
Law clerk for U.S. Supreme Court Justices Byron White and Ruth Bader Ginsburg.
Bachelor's degree, Swarthmore College; law degree, New York University School of Law.

record.title: Lawsuit against new federal tariffs
record.detail: Joined a multistate coalition of attorneys general suing to block President Trump's tariff increases, calling them illegal.

record.title: Opposition to King Soopers/Albertsons-Kroger merger
record.detail: As attorney general, helped stop the proposed King Soopers (Kroger)/Safeway (Albertsons) grocery merger.

record.title: Opioid settlement funds
record.detail: Says his office secured more than $900 million in opioid settlement funds from pharmaceutical companies for Colorado.

record.title: Multistate lawsuit against Meta
record.detail: Led or joined a 35-state lawsuit against Meta over the effect of social media design on young people; a settlement in that litigation was referenced in August 2026 coverage.

record.title: Lawsuits against the second Trump administration
record.detail: Says he has filed more than 60 lawsuits against the Trump administration as attorney general and would continue challenging federal actions he views as unlawful as governor.

research_notes: Weiser explicitly declined to take a position on the graduated state income tax ballot measure (then 'Proposed Initiative 195,' now Amendment 87) in the Aug. 27, 2026 debate with Lopez, saying 'I don't take positions until something is actually certified' (montrosepress.com/coloradopolitics.com coverage of that debate) -- so graduated-income-tax and income-tax-cap are left uncoded rather than stretched from that non-answer. No fetched source was found with his position on natural-gas-right (Amendment 82), conservation-sales-tax (Prop 137), mail-ballot-id, plain-language-ballots, redistricting-commission, keep-mail-voting, fentanyl-penalties, child-trafficking-life, sports-biological-sex, or deportation-priority; these are left out of positions rather than guessed. The clean-energy-shift coding reflects a genuine tension between his campaign platform's emission-reduction and solar/wind language and his more open-ended answer on continued oil and gas drilling in an Oct. 10, 2026 Colorado Sun interview; a reviewer may want to weigh those differently. Campaign finance totals for the 2026 governor's race were mentioned in web search summaries but no specific TRACER or news figure with a full citation was located in a fetched page, so finance is null. Build review 2026-10-14: removed the hunting-right position. In the June 24, 2026 Colorado Sun guide Weiser said he would listen to backers and opponents before deciding, which is not yet a position. Second pass 2026-10-14: added conservation-sales-tax from https://coloradosun.com/2026/09/30/proposition-137-colorado-conservation-wildfire-funding/.
